Use ORS (Oral Rehydration Salt) sachets available at any pharmacy or government health centre: dissolve one sachet in the amount of clean water shown on the packet (usually 200 ml or 1 litre) and sip frequently
If ORS sachets are not available, a homemade alternative can be used temporarily: add a pinch of salt and a small amount of sugar to a glass of clean water, stir well, and sip frequently
Other suitable homemade fluids: salted rice water, salted yogurt drink (lassi with salt), vegetable or chicken soup with salt, unsweetened fresh fruit juice, coconut water
Give extra fluids after each loose stool, adults should drink at least 200 ml after each episode

Diarrhea means three or more loose or watery stools per day. Acute diarrhea lasts less than 14 days. Diarrhea lasting more than 14 days is persistent diarrhea. Dysentery means blood is present in the stools.

Pinch the skin on the abdomen between two fingers, hold for one second, then let go. Watch how quickly it returns to normal: if it goes back immediately, no significant dehydration; if it stays raised for a brief instant, some dehydration, needs ORS urgently; if it goes back very slowly, taking more than 2 seconds, severe dehydration, go to hospital immediately.

Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral fever. Suspect dengue if a person has fever and two or more of the following: nausea, vomiting, rash, muscle pain, headache, pain behind the eyes, joint pain, or unusual bleeding, especially if they live in or recently travelled to a dengue-prone area.

Dengue must be managed under medical supervision with daily monitoring of blood counts and clinical status. Do not treat dengue at home beyond basic supportive care. The transition from mild to severe dengue can happen quickly.

Dry the skin thoroughly after bathing, especially the area between the toes and skin folds
Wash clothes separately in hot water and dry them inside-out in the sun
Do not share towels, clothes, or undergarments with others
Do not re-wear clothes before washing them

Hypoglycaemia (low blood sugar), symptoms: trembling or shaking, sudden sweating, anxiety or irritability, confusion, fast heartbeat, dizziness, blurred vision, weakness, seizures, or unconsciousness. These can occur if a person with diabetes skips meals or takes too much diabetes medicine. Immediate action: if the person is conscious and able to swallow, give sugar immediately, loose sugar, a sweet biscuit, misri (rock candy), or any sweet drink. If unconscious, do not give anything by mouth, go to hospital immediately.
Very high blood sugar with confusion, rapid breathing, and extreme thirst, may indicate diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), which is a medical emergency
Chest pain or severe breathlessness in a person with diabetes, diabetes significantly increases the risk of heart attack
Stroke warning signs in a person with diabetes: sudden one-sided weakness, speech difficulty, severe headache, vision loss, go to hospital immediately
Non-healing wound or foot ulcer with spreading redness, swelling, pus, or bad smell, diabetic foot infections can become life-threatening quickly
High fever with severe infection signs in a diabetic person, diabetes worsens the severity of infections
Take your diabetes medicines exactly as prescribed by your doctor, do not stop or change the dose on your own
Eat regular meals at consistent times, skipping meals can cause low blood sugar in those on certain diabetes medicines
Always carry something sweet (sugar, misri, a biscuit) in case of low blood sugar symptoms
Follow a diet low in refined sugar, white rice, maida, and sweet drinks. Eat more vegetables, whole grains, pulses, and fruits in moderate amounts
Be physically active, at least 30 minutes of walking or light exercise daily helps control blood sugar
Do not smoke, smoking dramatically increases the risk of heart attack and kidney damage in diabetics
Avoid alcohol or use it very minimally
Inspect your feet every day for cuts, blisters, redness, swelling, or wounds, even small injuries can become serious in diabetics
Wear proper footwear at all times, avoid going barefoot
Monitor your blood sugar regularly as advised by your doctor
Keep all follow-up appointments, diabetes requires regular monitoring of blood sugar, blood pressure, kidney function, and eyes

Blood sugar reading on a home glucometer that is consistently high

Sore throat is pain in the throat on swallowing. It may be caused by a virus (most common) or bacteria. Viral sore throats do not need antibiotics. Bacterial sore throat (streptococcal) has specific features and needs a doctor to decide on treatment.
Crusted (Norwegian) scabies: thick, yellow-brown crusts on the skin, particularly on the hands and feet, this is a severe form seen in people with weak immunity and is highly contagious
Signs of secondary bacterial infection: skin that is red, swollen, warm, and has pus or a foul smell
Scabies in someone who is immunocompromised (on steroids, with HIV, or on chemotherapy), this can become very severe quickly

All family members and close physical contacts must be treated at the same time, even if they have no symptoms, treating only the affected person will lead to re-infestation
Wash all clothes, towels, and bedlinen used in the past three days in hot water and dry them in the sun
Items that cannot be washed (shoes, bags) can be sealed in a plastic bag for at least 3 days, the mite cannot survive without human contact
Do not share clothing, towels, or bedding with others during the infestation
Maintain good general hygiene throughout treatment
Important: itching can continue for several weeks after successful treatment, this is normal and does not mean the treatment has failed
Do not repeat the treatment application just because itching continues, continue antihistamines for relief instead

Urticaria: Sudden appearance of raised, itchy welts (wheals) on the skin of variable size and shape, surrounded by redness. Individual welts usually resolve within 1 to 24 hours but new ones may keep appearing. Chronic urticaria means it has lasted more than 6 weeks.

Angioedema: Sudden, deep swelling of the skin, often affecting the face, lips, tongue, throat, or genitals. It can take up to 72 hours to resolve. When it affects the throat or airway, it is a medical emergency.
